steps.en: Pulmonary pressure by echo is a velocity plus a venous pressure. The tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity reflects the systolic pressure drop from right ventricle to right atrium, so four times velocity squared plus right atrial pressure from the cava gives systolic pulmonary artery pressure. A pulmonary regurgitant jet extends the same logic to mean and diastolic pressure. The estimate screens for pulmonary hypertension and follows it, but it is not a catheter: a faint envelope, a bad angle or a wrong atrial pressure all move the number. In India long standing rheumatic mitral stenosis is a leading cause of raised pulmonary pressure, often with a D shaped septum and a struggling right heart.
Find the tricuspid jet on colour in the view that shows it best: apical four chamber, right ventricle inflow or parasternal short axis.
Align continuous wave along the jet and record the densest envelope with the sharpest peak from every window.
Take the peak velocity of the best envelope only, never an average of windows.
Estimate right atrial pressure from caval size and sniff collapse by the caval lesson.
Add 4 times velocity squared to the atrial pressure for systolic pulmonary pressure.
Check the septal shape, right heart size and pulmonary regurgitant velocity as supporting evidence.
Reporting a faint partial envelope as the pressure. Fix: Try the next window and optimise gain. The true peak lives where alignment is best, and underreading hides hypertension.
Tracing gain noise above the true peak. Fix: Trace the dense modal edge only. Feathering and noise sit above the true peak.
Skipping the jet because colour looks trivial. Fix: A loud murmur with a tiny jet can still carry high velocity, so chase the signal rather than the colour size.
Trusting the peak in torrential tricuspid regurgitation. Fix: Severe free tricuspid regurgitation equalises pressures early and blunts the peak, so read pressure with the clinical picture.
Systolic pulmonary pressure formula. 4 times tricuspid velocity squared plus right atrial pressure. Source: ASE right heart assessment, section on pulmonary pressures

Tricuspid velocity suggesting pulmonary hypertension. Peak velocity above 2.8 m per s deserves further assessment. Source: ASE and EACVI 2016 diastolic function, section on pulmonary pressures, and ESC pulmonary hypertension guidance, in own words
Right atrial pressure terms. About 3, 8 or 15 mmHg from caval size with sniff collapse. Source: ASE right heart assessment, section on inferior vena cava and right atrial pressure
Supporting mean pressure clue. Pulmonary regurgitant end diastolic velocity plus atrial pressure estimates diastolic pressure. Source: ASE right heart assessment, section on pulmonary regurgitation
Agitated saline or contrast sharpens a faint envelope when pressure matters for a decision.
High cardiac output raises velocity without vascular disease, so read pressure with flow state.
Serial estimates need the same window and rhythm, or trends mislead.

q.en: How is systolic pulmonary pressure estimated?

o.en: 4 times velocity squared plus atrial pressure

why.en: The tricuspid peak gives the ventriculo atrial drop as 4 v squared, and adding right atrial pressure from the cava yields systolic pulmonary pressure.

q.en: Which tricuspid velocity triggers pulmonary hypertension assessment?

why.en: Above 2.8 m per s the probability of pulmonary hypertension rises enough to deserve full assessment.

q.en: Which envelope gives the peak velocity?

o.en: The densest envelope with the sharpest peak

why.en: Only the best aligned densest envelope holds the true peak; averaging or tracing noise corrupts the estimate.

q.en: An Indian patient shows raised pulmonary pressure with a D shaped septum and a huge left atrium. What fits best?

o.en: Rheumatic mitral stenosis with a D shaped septum

why.en: Long standing rheumatic mitral stenosis raises pulmonary venous then arterial pressure, flattening the septum and straining the right heart.
